summary:
EarthPulse is an interactive Earth-observation web platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing the "Dancing with the SARs" challenge through water and wetlands monitoring.

Our project makes NASA–ISRO NISAR radar observations easier to explore and understand. Using satellite observations of Tanguar Haor, Bangladesh, between 2 observation date , users can compare radar imagery, investigate surface backscatter changes, and view statistics through interactive maps and charts.

EarthPulse helps make complex satellite data accessible to students, researchers, and communities while clearly communicating scientific uncertainty. It demonstrates radar-based environmental change exploration rather than claiming validated flood detection.
details:
Project Overview

EarthPulse is a web-based environmental observation platform that transforms complex satellite radar measurements into accessible maps, visual comparisons, and understandable statistics.

How It Works

The platform processes two supplied NASA–ISRO NISAR L2 GCOV radar observations covering Tanguar Haor, Bangladesh, dated October 6 and October 30, 2026 and more other date .

Radar intensity data is processed using Python, NumPy, and Rasterio to calculate backscatter differences and generate visual layers and descriptive statistics.

Main Features

  • Interactive geographic maps with before, after, swipe, and radar-change visualization.
  • Exploration of NASA satellite observations through an observation calendar.
  • Statistical insights, charts, histograms, and radar intensity comparisons.
  • Additional NASA MODIS Terra optical imagery for visual context.
  • Guided explanations of radar measurements, data provenance, and scientific limitations.
  • Responsive web interface for desktop and mobile users.

Technologies Used

Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet, Recharts, Python, NumPy, and Rasterio. The website is deployed using Vercel.

Scientific Limitations

The application measures radar backscatter differences, not validated flood extent. Its exploratory change thresholds do not establish water classification, and missing acquisition metadata and quality masks limit scientific interpretation.

Project Impact

EarthPulse demonstrates how satellite observations can become more understandable, transparent, and accessible. Future work could incorporate independently validated water-classification data and additional observations to support more rigorous environmental monitoring.
